newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish Liberals call for 1997 tax, spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Danish Liberals call for 1997 tax, spending cuts.

text.p: Denmark's main opposition Liberal Party called on Monday for widespread cuts in 1997 welfare, adult education and overseas aid spending while proposing tax cuts and incentives to industry and business.

Publishing its proposals for the 1997 state budget -- traditionally a compromise between the minority government and leading opposition parties -- the Liberals outlined gross cuts of 27 billion crowns, mainly in the lavish benefits system.
The Social Democrat-led government last month published its draft 1997 budget, showing a state deficit of 21.5 billion crowns, which the Liberal plan would reduce to 9.1 billion.

Monday's Liberal proposal outlines reductions of 5.8 billion in unemployment benefits and streamlining the welfare system. It also sees 170,000 new jobs created by the year 2,000 while at the same time, freezing public sector hiring.
It wants 4.2 billion crowns cut from the foreign aid budget and 4.4 billion in government subsidies to business ended.

The Liberals also seek reductions in state support to political parties and trades unions, paid leave and retraining schemes and sees cost-cutting opportunities in streamlining central and local government bureacracy.
They want 13.6 billion crowns spent on tax cuts and 1.1 billion in other spending, giving a net savings of 12.4 billion.
Last year, the government's plan for a 33. 5 billion crown budget deficit was revised to a 28.8 billion crown shortfall after protracted negotiations with the Liberals and their Conservative allies.

Relations between the two main opposition parties, partners in a series of coalition governments from 1982 to 1993, soured when the Conservatives made a separate budget deal with the government, upsetting the Liberals who wanted to hold out for deeper welfare cuts.
The 1997 budget is liable to be the subject of extensive political haggling over the next two or three months but to be ratified by parliament by December.
